q: What is the difference between an image and a container?
opts: An image is running; a container is a blueprint
An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance
A container is stored on disk; an image runs in memory
exp: A Docker image is a read-only blueprint built from a Dockerfile. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of that image — like a class vs an object in OOP.

q: What does docker ps -a show?
exp: docker ps shows only running containers. The -a (--all) flag includes stopped, exited, and paused containers too.

q: What does the -d flag do in docker run -d nginx?
opts: Deletes the container after it exits
Runs the container in detached (background) mode
exp: -d (--detach) starts the container in the background. Without it, your terminal attaches to the container stdout/stderr. Use docker logs to view output of detached containers.

q: What command removes all stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, and build cache?
exp: docker system prune is the single command to reclaim disk space. Add -a to also remove unused images, and --volumes to remove unused volumes.

q: Which command shows the layers of a Docker image?
exp: docker history <image> shows each layer: the command that created it, its size, and when it was created. Useful for understanding image composition and finding bloated layers.

q: What is a dangling image?
opts: An image with no tags no longer referenced by any container
An image that failed to build
exp: Dangling images are untagged, unreferenced image layers (shown as <none>:<none>). They accumulate during builds when the same tag is rebuilt. Clean up with docker image prune.

q: How do you follow the live logs of a running container?
exp: docker logs -f (--follow) streams live logs. Add --tail 100 to start with the last 100 lines. docker attach connects to the main process which can interfere.

q: What does docker inspect return?
opts: A JSON blob of low-level configuration details
exp: docker inspect returns detailed JSON metadata about a container or image: network settings, mounts, environment variables, state, labels, and more.

q: What does the --rm flag do in docker run?
opts: Automatically removes the container when it exits
exp: --rm automatically deletes the container when it exits. Great for one-off commands and CI jobs where you do not want to accumulate stopped containers.

q: Which command copies a file from a running container to the host?
exp: docker cp <container>:<src_path> <dst_path> copies files between a container and the host filesystem. Works in both directions.

q: What does docker stats show?
opts: Live CPU, memory, network I/O stats for running containers
exp: docker stats streams real-time resource usage: CPU %, memory usage/limit, net I/O, block I/O, and PIDs for each running container.

q: What is the purpose of docker commit?
opts: Save container changes as a new image
Push an image to a registry
exp: docker commit creates a new image from a containers current state. Useful for debugging but avoid for production — use Dockerfiles for reproducible builds.

q: What does docker system df show?
exp: docker system df shows disk space used by images, containers, volumes, and build cache — useful for knowing what is safe to prune.

q: What does docker tag do?
opts: Creates an alias/tag pointing to an existing image
exp: docker tag <source> <target> creates a new tag pointing to the same image layers. No data is copied — tags are just references.

q: What is the difference between docker stop and docker kill?
opts: docker stop sends SIGTERM then waits; docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately
docker kill is for images; docker stop is for containers
docker stop removes the container; docker kill only pauses it
exp: docker stop sends SIGTERM allowing graceful shutdown, then SIGKILL after a timeout (default 10s). docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately — no cleanup possible.

q: How do you view all available Docker commands?
exp: docker --help lists top-level commands. docker <command> --help gives detailed help for any specific command, including flags and examples.

q: What format does docker inspect --format use?
exp: docker inspect --format uses Go template syntax. Example: docker inspect --format="{{.State.Status}}" mycontainer outputs just the status field.

q: What does docker events stream?
opts: Real-time events from the Docker daemon (start, stop, pull, etc.)
exp: docker events streams real-time events from the Docker daemon: container lifecycle events, image pulls, network creation, volume mounts, and more.

q: What does docker top do?
opts: Lists running processes inside a container
Displays the Docker daemon top-level info
exp: docker top <container> displays running processes inside a container, similar to the Unix top/ps command. Useful for quick process inspection without exec-ing in.

q: How do you pass environment variables to a container at runtime?
opts: Environment variables cannot be passed at runtime
exp: Use -e KEY=VALUE or --env KEY=VALUE flags. For many vars, use --env-file .env to load from a file. These override ENV values set in the Dockerfile.

q: What is the purpose of ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?
opts: Defines the executable to run when the container starts
exp: ENTRYPOINT defines the main process. Unlike CMD, it cannot be overridden at runtime (only appended to). Combined with CMD, it creates flexible entry points.

q: Which combination gives best layer caching for a Node.js app?
opts: COPY package*.json ./ then RUN npm install then COPY . .
They all produce the same cache behavior
exp: Copy only package files first, install dependencies (cached unless package.json changes), then copy source code. Code changes do not bust the npm install cache.

q: What does the HEALTHCHECK instruction do?
opts: Checks if the Dockerfile is valid
Tells Docker how to test if a container is working
exp: HEALTHCHECK runs a command inside the container periodically. If it fails repeatedly, the container is marked unhealthy. Orchestrators use this to manage traffic routing.

q: What is a multi-stage build used for?
opts: Build images for multiple CPU architectures
Reduce final image size by separating build and runtime stages
exp: Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM statements. Build tools live in early stages. The final stage copies only the compiled artifact — dramatically reducing image size.

q: What is the difference between RUN, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT?
opts: RUN executes during build; CMD is default command at startup; ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable
CMD executes at build time; RUN and ENTRYPOINT are runtime
RUN is for Linux; CMD is for Windows
exp: RUN executes during build (creates layers). CMD provides default arguments at startup (overridable). ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed executable (not overridable without --entrypoint).

q: What does ARG differ from ENV in a Dockerfile?
opts: ARG variables persist in the final image; ENV does not
ENV is only available at build time; ARG persists at runtime
ARG is only available during build; ENV persists into the running container
exp: ARG variables exist only during the build process (not in the final image). ENV variables persist into the container runtime. Use ARG for build-time config, ENV for runtime config.

q: What is the best base image for a production Node.js app?
exp: node:20-alpine (~7MB) vs node:20 (~900MB, Debian). Always pin to a specific version (not latest) and prefer alpine or slim variants in production.

q: What does WORKDIR do in a Dockerfile?
opts: Sets the working directory for subsequent instructions
exp: WORKDIR sets the working directory for RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, and ADD instructions. If the directory does not exist, Docker creates it automatically.

q: What is the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?
opts: ADD can fetch remote URLs and auto-extract archives; COPY just copies local files
COPY is faster; ADD is more secure
ADD works for directories; COPY only for files
exp: COPY is the preferred instruction for copying local files. ADD has extra magic: it can fetch remote URLs and auto-extract tar archives. Best practice: use COPY unless you specifically need ADD features.

q: What does FROM scratch mean in a Dockerfile?
opts: Start from the latest Ubuntu image
Start from an empty base with no OS layer
Start from the Docker scratch registry
Scratch is an alias for alpine
exp: FROM scratch creates a truly minimal image with no base OS. Used for static binaries (like Go apps) that have no runtime dependencies. Results in the smallest possible images.

q: How do you reduce RUN layers in a Dockerfile?
opts: Chain commands with && in a single RUN instruction
exp: Each RUN creates a new layer. Chain commands with && and use \ for line continuation: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

q: What does .dockerignore do?
opts: Lists files to delete from the image
Excludes files and directories from the build context sent to the Docker daemon
Defines ignore patterns for docker logs
exp: .dockerignore works like .gitignore for Docker builds. It prevents files from being sent to the daemon in the build context, speeding up builds and preventing secrets from leaking.

q: What is the purpose of EXPOSE in a Dockerfile?
opts: Opens the port on the host automatically
Documents that the container listens on that port — does NOT publish it
Maps the port to a random host port
exp: EXPOSE is documentation only. It tells Docker and developers what port the app listens on but does NOT publish it to the host. Use -p or ports: in compose to actually publish.

q: What is a distroless image?
opts: An image without a package manager
An image containing only the application and its runtime dependencies, no shell or OS utilities
An image built without a Dockerfile
A Docker Hub term for unverified images
exp: Distroless images (by Google) contain only the app and runtime libraries — no shell, no package manager, no system utilities. Extremely small and secure, but harder to debug.

q: What does LABEL do in a Dockerfile?
opts: Adds metadata key-value pairs to the image
Tags the image for a registry
exp: LABEL adds metadata to an image as key-value pairs: maintainer, version, description, etc. Access them with docker inspect. Good for image cataloging and tooling.

q: What is BuildKit and why use it?
opts: Dockers next-generation build engine with parallelism, caching, and secret support
exp: BuildKit is Docker modern build engine. It enables parallel stage execution, improved caching, build secrets (no secret leakage in layers), SSH forwarding, and --cache-from/--cache-to.

q: What does SHELL instruction do in a Dockerfile?
opts: Opens a shell in the container
Changes the default shell used for RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT shell form
exp: SHELL changes the default shell for subsequent RUN/CMD/ENTRYPOINT instructions. Default is ["/bin/sh", "-c"]. Use SHELL ["powershell", "-command"] for Windows containers.

q: What is the exec form vs shell form for CMD?
opts: Exec form [cmd,arg] runs directly; shell form cmd arg runs via shell — affecting signal handling
Exec form only works on Linux
exp: Exec form CMD ["node","app.js"] runs the process directly (PID 1, receives signals correctly). Shell form CMD node app.js wraps in /bin/sh -c, so the shell is PID 1 and signals may not propagate.

q: How do you pass build-time secrets securely with BuildKit?
opts: Use --build-arg and hope for the best
Use RUN --mount=type=secret which never appears in image layers
Write to a file and COPY it
exp: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mysecret cat /run/secrets/mysecret mounts a secret temporarily during build. The secret never appears in image layers, unlike --build-arg which is cached.

q: What does STOPSIGNAL do in a Dockerfile?
opts: Defines the signal Docker sends to stop the container
exp: STOPSIGNAL sets the system call signal sent to the container to exit. Default is SIGTERM. Some apps handle SIGUSR1 or SIGINT better for graceful shutdown.

q: What does docker run -p 8080:80 mean?
opts: Maps container port 8080 to host port 80
Maps host port 8080 to container port 80
Creates a network bridge between the ports
exp: Format is -p HOST:CONTAINER. So -p 8080:80 means traffic hitting port 8080 on your host machine is forwarded to port 80 inside the container.

q: What is the default network driver for containers on a single host?
exp: By default, Docker uses the bridge driver. Each bridge network gets its own subnet and Docker acts as a DNS resolver for container names within the same network.

q: What network mode gives a container direct access to the host network stack?
exp: --network host removes network isolation. The container shares the host network namespace directly. Great for performance-sensitive tools but breaks container portability.

q: What is an overlay network in Docker used for?
opts: Connecting containers on the same host
Connecting containers across multiple Docker hosts (Swarm)
Creating isolated networks with no external access
Connecting Docker to the host network
exp: Overlay networks span multiple Docker daemons, allowing containers on different hosts in a Swarm to communicate as if on the same local network. Backed by VXLAN tunneling.

q: What does --network none do when running a container?
opts: Removes all network interfaces from the container
exp: --network none disables all networking for the container. The container gets no network interface except loopback. Useful for air-gapped processing tasks.

q: How do containers on the same Docker network resolve each other?
opts: By container or service name via Docker internal DNS
exp: Docker has a built-in DNS server for user-defined networks. Containers can resolve each other by container name (or service name in Compose) automatically.

q: What is macvlan networking in Docker?
opts: Assigns each container its own MAC address, making it appear as a physical device on the network
exp: macvlan assigns each container a MAC address and connects it directly to the physical network. Containers appear as separate physical devices. Useful for legacy apps needing direct L2 access.

q: What happens to container DNS when you use --network host?
opts: The container uses the host DNS settings directly
A custom DNS resolver is used
exp: With --network host, the container shares the host network namespace completely, including DNS. It reads /etc/resolv.conf from the host directly.

q: How do you connect a running container to an additional network?
exp: docker network connect <network> <container> attaches a running container to another network without restarting it. The container then has interfaces on both networks.

q: What port does Docker internal DNS listen on?
exp: Docker internal DNS resolver listens on port 53 inside the container. When a container does a DNS lookup, queries go to 127.0.0.11:53 (the embedded DNS server) on user-defined networks.

q: What is the difference between published and exposed ports?
opts: EXPOSE documents the port; -p/ports: publishes it to the host
EXPOSE opens firewall rules; -p adds metadata
Published ports are for external traffic; exposed ports are internal only
exp: EXPOSE is metadata only — no host binding. -p HOST:CONTAINER (or ports: in Compose) actually binds the container port to a host port, making it accessible externally.

q: How do you publish a container port to a random available host port?
opts: docker run -P nginx uses EXPOSE ports
Both A and B are correct
exp: -p :80 or -P both work. -P publishes all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports. Use docker port <container> to see which random port was assigned.

q: What is the docker0 bridge?
opts: The default bridge network created by Docker daemon
exp: docker0 is the default bridge network interface created by Docker daemon on the host. Containers on the default bridge network connect through docker0, typically using 172.17.0.0/16 subnet.

q: Why should you use user-defined networks instead of the default bridge?
opts: User-defined networks provide automatic DNS resolution by container name; default bridge uses only IP
The default bridge does not support multiple containers
exp: On the default bridge, containers communicate by IP only. On user-defined bridge networks, Docker provides DNS so containers resolve each other by name — a critical difference for multi-container apps.

q: What does --publish-all (-P) do?
opts: Publishes all EXPOSEd ports to random ephemeral ports on the host
exp: -P (--publish-all) publishes every port listed in EXPOSE to a random available port on the host. Use docker port <container> to see the mapping.

q: What is the key difference between a volume and a bind mount?
opts: Volumes are slower; bind mounts are faster
Volumes are managed by Docker; bind mounts link to a specific host path
Bind mounts persist data; volumes are ephemeral
exp: Volumes are managed by Docker (/var/lib/docker/volumes/) — portable, shareable, easy to back up. Bind mounts directly mount a host directory path into the container.

q: What happens to data in a container with no volumes when deleted?
opts: It is saved to the host automatically
It is moved to a dangling volume
It is backed up to an image layer
exp: Container filesystems are ephemeral. Without a volume or bind mount, all writes go to the writable container layer, which is destroyed when the container is removed.

q: What is the correct way to share data between two containers?
opts: Use a named volume mounted in both containers
exp: Named volumes can be mounted into multiple containers simultaneously, allowing shared data. Both containers reference the same volume name in their run/compose config.

q: What is a tmpfs mount?
opts: A temporary volume stored on disk
An in-memory filesystem that disappears when the container stops
exp: tmpfs mounts store data in host memory only — never written to disk. Fast and ephemeral. Great for sensitive data (tokens, secrets) that should not persist or hit disk.

q: Where does Docker store named volumes by default on Linux?
exp: Docker stores named volume data in /var/lib/docker/volumes/<volume_name>/_data on Linux. You can inspect a volume with docker volume inspect to find the exact Mountpoint.

q: What does docker volume prune do?
opts: Removes all volumes including named ones
Removes only anonymous volumes not used by any container
exp: docker volume prune removes all anonymous (unnamed) volumes not currently used by any container. Named volumes are NOT removed unless you use --all flag.

q: What is a volume driver in Docker?
opts: A plugin that lets Docker volumes use external storage (NFS, AWS EBS, etc.)
The Docker daemon component managing volumes
exp: Volume drivers are plugins extending Dockers volume system. They allow volumes to be backed by external storage: NFS, cloud block storage (EBS, GCE PD), distributed filesystems, etc.

q: What is the difference between anonymous and named volumes?
opts: Named volumes are specified with a name; anonymous volumes get a random ID and are harder to manage
Anonymous volumes persist; named volumes are temporary
exp: Named volumes (docker run -v mydata:/app/data) are easy to reference and manage. Anonymous volumes (-v /app/data) get a random ID hash — hard to identify and reuse.

q: How do you back up a Docker volume?
opts: Run a temporary container that mounts the volume and tars it to the host
Docker volumes cannot be backed up
exp: Common pattern: docker run --rm -v myvolume:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz /data. This mounts the volume and archives it to the host.

q: What does --mount vs -v do differently?
opts: --mount is more verbose and explicit; -v is shorthand with implicit behavior
exp: --mount is explicit and readable: --mount type=volume,source=myvol,target=/data. -v is shorthand: -v myvol:/data. --mount fails fast on missing dirs; -v creates them. Docker recommends --mount.

q: What does depends_on guarantee in Docker Compose?
opts: The dependent service is healthy before starting
Container startup order only — not that the service is ready
exp: depends_on only controls start order. Use depends_on with condition: service_healthy and a healthcheck to wait until a service is actually ready to accept connections.

q: In Docker Compose, how do containers resolve each other by hostname?
opts: By service name defined in compose.yaml
By container name with a random suffix
exp: Docker Compose creates a default network and sets up DNS so containers can reach each other using the service name (e.g., db, redis, app) as the hostname.

q: What does restart: always do in Docker Compose?
opts: Restarts the container on a schedule
Restarts the container whenever it exits, regardless of exit code
exp: restart: always makes Docker always restart the container when it exits (including on daemon startup after a host reboot). Use unless-stopped to not restart when manually stopped.

q: What is the purpose of a healthcheck in Compose with depends_on?
opts: Ensure a service is fully ready before dependent services start
exp: With depends_on condition: service_healthy, Docker waits until the dependencys healthcheck passes before starting the dependent service. Essential for databases that need time to initialize.

q: What is a Compose profile used for?
opts: To selectively start a subset of services using --profile flag
exp: Profiles let you group optional services. E.g., a debug profile runs only when explicitly enabled: docker compose --profile debug up. Core services run always; profiled services run on demand.

q: What does docker compose down -v do?
opts: Stops and removes containers, networks, and also named volumes
exp: docker compose down removes containers and networks. Adding -v also removes named volumes defined in the compose file. Warning: this permanently deletes volume data.

q: What is a compose override file?
opts: A file that replaces the main compose.yaml
docker-compose.override.yaml is auto-merged, allowing environment-specific overrides
A file used only in production
A Compose v1 concept removed in v2
exp: docker-compose.override.yaml is automatically merged with docker-compose.yaml. Use it for local dev overrides (volume mounts, debug ports) without modifying the main file.

q: How do you scale a service to 3 replicas in Compose?
opts: Add replicas: 3 to the service config
exp: Both work. docker compose up --scale app=3 at runtime, or add deploy: replicas: 3 in the compose.yaml (requires Swarm or Compose v3). The --scale flag is common for local testing.

q: What is the build context in a compose service?
opts: The directory sent to Docker daemon when building — typically the service directory
exp: The build context (build: . or build: context: ./myservice) defines which directory is sent to the Docker daemon. The Dockerfile is looked up there by default.

q: What does the volumes: top-level key in compose.yaml define?
opts: Volume mounts for a specific service
Named volumes that can be shared across services
exp: Top-level volumes: declares named volumes managed by Docker. Individual services reference them in their own volumes: section. They persist across docker compose down (unless -v is used).

q: What does env_file do in a compose service?
opts: Loads environment variables from one or more external files
Sets the .env file path for variable substitution
exp: env_file: .env.production loads KEY=VALUE pairs from a file into the container environment. Different from .env which handles variable substitution in compose.yaml itself.

q: What is the difference between expose and ports in compose?
opts: expose makes ports available between services; ports publishes to the host
expose is for external traffic; ports is internal
exp: expose: [3000] makes port 3000 available to other services on the network but NOT the host. ports: - "3000:3000" publishes to the host. Use expose for internal-only services.

q: How do you view logs for a specific service in Compose?
exp: docker compose logs <service> shows logs for that service. Add -f to follow and --tail N to limit output. Without a service name, it shows all services interleaved.

q: What is the networks: top-level key used for in compose?
opts: Define which networks each service uses
Create named networks with custom drivers, IPAM, and settings
exp: The top-level networks: key creates named networks that services can join. You can configure driver (bridge/overlay), IPAM (custom subnets), labels, and whether to use an external pre-existing network.

q: What does docker compose exec vs docker compose run do?
opts: exec runs a command in an existing running container; run starts a new one-off container
run is for services; exec is for containers
exp: docker compose exec runs a command in an already-running service container. docker compose run starts a fresh container for a one-off command. run containers are removed with --rm.

q: Why should you avoid running containers as root?
opts: If the container is compromised, the attacker gains root access on the host
Docker does not support running as root
exp: A root process in a container, if it escapes the container namespace, has root on the host. Always use USER to specify a non-root user in your Dockerfile.

q: What is the risk of COPY . . without .dockerignore?
opts: Sensitive files like .env and node_modules get copied into the image
It makes the build slower only
exp: .dockerignore works like .gitignore. Without it, COPY . . can include .git, .env files, node_modules, and other sensitive or large directories into the image.

q: What does the --read-only flag do?
opts: Makes the container filesystem read-only, preventing writes
exp: --read-only mounts the containers root filesystem as read-only. Combined with --tmpfs for temp files, this is a strong hardening technique that prevents runtime modification.

q: What is the principle of least privilege in Docker?
opts: Use the smallest possible base image
Give containers only the permissions and capabilities they need
exp: Least privilege means containers run as non-root, drop unnecessary Linux capabilities (--cap-drop ALL, --cap-add only what is needed), use read-only filesystems, and limit resource access.

q: What does --privileged do when running a container?
opts: Grants admin access to Docker Hub
Gives the container full access to host devices and disables security profiles
exp: --privileged gives the container nearly unrestricted access to the host: all capabilities, all devices, no seccomp/AppArmor. Avoid in production — use specific --cap-add and --device instead.

q: What is seccomp in the context of Docker security?
opts: A Linux syscall filtering mechanism that limits which system calls a container can make
exp: Seccomp (secure computing mode) is a Linux kernel feature. Docker applies a default seccomp profile that blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls. You can apply custom profiles or disable it (not recommended).

q: What tool is commonly used to scan Docker images for CVEs?
opts: docker scan (powered by Snyk) or Trivy
exp: Trivy (by Aqua Security) and Snyk are the most popular. docker scout is Dockers built-in scanner. All scan image layers for known CVEs in OS packages and application dependencies.

q: Why is using :latest tag a security risk?
opts: It is not a security risk
latest can pull a different, potentially vulnerable image on each build/pull
Docker Hub blocks latest in production
exp: latest is mutable — it can point to a different image version anytime. Pin to specific versions (node:20.11.0-alpine) or digests (node@sha256:abc123) for reproducible, auditable builds.

q: What is a Docker content trust (DCT)?
opts: A framework for signing and verifying image integrity using Notary
exp: Docker Content Trust uses Notary to sign images. Enable with DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1. Only signed images can be pulled/run. Protects against supply chain attacks and tampered images.

q: What is the risk of storing secrets in ENV instructions?
opts: ENV values are baked into the image and visible in docker inspect and docker history
Only root can see ENV values
exp: ENV values persist in the image and are visible via docker inspect and docker history. Anyone with image access sees them. Use Docker secrets, vault solutions, or runtime --env injection instead.

q: What does --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE do?
opts: Drops all Linux capabilities then adds back only the ability to bind ports below 1024
exp: Best practice: drop ALL capabilities then add back only what the app needs. NET_BIND_SERVICE allows binding ports < 1024. Common caps: NET_BIND_SERVICE, CHOWN, SETUID, SETGID.

q: What is AppArmor in Docker context?
opts: A Linux MAC (Mandatory Access Control) system that restricts container actions via profiles
exp: AppArmor is a Linux security module. Docker applies a default AppArmor profile (docker-default) that restricts dangerous operations. Custom profiles provide fine-grained control over file access and capabilities.

q: What should you do before deploying a Docker image to production?
opts: Just run it — Docker is secure by default
Scan for CVEs, verify base image source, check for secrets in layers, ensure non-root user
Only check if it builds successfully
Just update to the latest base image
exp: Production checklist: CVE scan (Trivy/Scout), non-root user, no secrets in layers, pinned base image, minimal packages, read-only filesystem where possible, resource limits set.

q: What is a rootless Docker setup?
opts: Running the Docker daemon itself as a non-root user, eliminating daemon privilege escalation risk
A mode that disables all security features
exp: Rootless mode runs the Docker daemon and containers as a non-root user. If the daemon is compromised, the attacker does not gain root on the host. Supported since Docker 20.10.

q: What does USER 1000:1000 mean in a Dockerfile?
opts: Set the user and group ID for running the container process
exp: USER <uid>:<gid> sets the user and group for subsequent RUN/CMD/ENTRYPOINT instructions. Using numeric IDs (not names) works across images without requiring the user to exist in /etc/passwd.

q: What does the --no-new-privileges flag do?
opts: Prevents the container from installing new packages
Prevents container processes from gaining additional privileges via setuid/setgid binaries
exp: --security-opt no-new-privileges:true prevents container processes from escalating privileges via setuid/setgid binaries (like sudo). An important defense-in-depth measure.

q: What is image signing with Cosign?
opts: Cryptographically signing an image so consumers can verify it was not tampered with
exp: Cosign (by Sigstore) creates a cryptographic signature for an OCI image. Consumers verify the signature before pulling. Part of software supply chain security (SLSA compliance).

q: Why should you avoid ADD with remote URLs in Dockerfiles?
opts: Remote URLs bypass integrity verification — the content can change or be replaced with malicious content
Docker blocks remote URLs in ADD
exp: ADD https://example.com/file downloads a file without integrity verification. The URL content can change. Use RUN curl -fsSL <url> | sha256sum -c - to verify checksums explicitly.

q: What is the risk of exposing the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) to a container?
opts: The container can control the Docker daemon — effectively giving it root access to the host
exp: Mounting the Docker socket gives the container full control over Docker: it can spawn privileged containers, escape to host, delete volumes, read secrets from other containers. Avoid unless absolutely necessary.

q: What does docker bench security do?
opts: Runs a CIS Docker Benchmark audit of host and daemon configuration
exp: Docker Bench Security (github.com/docker/docker-bench-security) runs automated checks against CIS Docker Benchmark: daemon configuration, container runtime settings, image hygiene, and more.
